slides.title: [1] Re-state the problem, confirm two known costs
slides.code:
position_ideal = [0.15, 0.25, 0.45,   # bays 1-3
                  0.55, 0.35, 0.20]   # bays 4-6
panel_transmittance = [0.10, 0.20, 0.30,
                       0.40, 0.50, 0.60]  # 6 panels

def cost(perm: list) -> float:
    """Squared mismatch summed over all six bays."""
    return sum((panel_transmittance[p]
                - position_ideal[i]) ** 2
               for i, p in enumerate(perm))
print(round(cost((0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)), 4))
print(round(cost((0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1)), 4))
slides.explainBody: Same cost function, same two example permutations, same numbers: 0.2325 for 'panel i in bay i,' 0.0125 for the permutation Monday's brute force already proved optimal. The docstring and the parameter/return type hints are the Week 4 convention, not decoration — they are what the reader checks the function against. Recall from Monday: the sum(...) line is a GENERATOR EXPRESSION — 'for each bay i and its assigned panel p, compute one term, feed it straight into sum().' round(..., 4) is needed because the raw float prints as 0.23249999999999998.
slides.teaching: Ask students to predict both numbers from memory before running — most should recall 0.0125 from Monday without looking.

slides.title: Studio 1: confirm before building anything new
slides.prompt: A pipeline you cannot trust from its own first cell is not worth building on.
steps: Predict cost((0,1,2,3,4,5)) from memory before running.
Run cell [1] and compare.
Confirm perm is a genuine PERMUTATION - no repeated panel index, no skipped one.
State in one sentence why this cost function alone cannot tell you which arrangement is best - you still need to search.
slides.teaching: This matters because every bug later in the studio (including the AI-audit) traces back to breaking this one guarantee: perm must stay a valid permutation.

slides.title: [2] Re-run brute force, and time it
slides.code:
import itertools, time

t0 = time.perf_counter()
all_perms = list(itertools.permutations(range(6)))
costs = [cost(p) for p in all_perms]
t1 = time.perf_counter()

best = all_perms[costs.index(min(costs))]
print(len(all_perms), 'perms in',
      round((t1 - t0) * 1000, 2), 'ms')
print('best:', best, 'cost:', round(min(costs), 4))
slides.explainBody: 720 permutations checked in about 1 millisecond on this machine — your own timing will differ by machine, but the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE (a fraction of a second, for N=6) will not. Keep this number; it is the baseline the GA is compared against a few cells from now.
slides.teaching: Have students record their own machine's millisecond reading — the exact number does not matter, only that it stays small.

slides.title: Studio 2: verify against Monday's numbers
slides.prompt: A number that changed between Monday and today, unexplained, is a bug, not a coincidence.
steps: Confirm 720 permutations checked - 6! by hand.
Confirm best cost 0.0125 matches Monday's deck exactly.
Record your own machine's timing in milliseconds.
State one sentence: why is checking every option still fine at N=6, but not at N=12?
slides.teaching: Expected answer to step 4: 12! is about 479 million — checking every option would take far too long, no matter how fast the machine.

slides.title: Predict: does the recap get stuck again?
slides.code:
end, end_cost = hill_climb([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print('stuck at:', end, 'cost:', round(end_cost, 4))
slides.question: Same call as Monday's demo. What does this print?
options: stuck at: [0, 1, 2, 5, 4, 3] cost: 0.0925 -- same local optimum as Monday
stuck at: (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1) cost: 0.0125 -- the true optimum
stuck at: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] cost: 0.2325 -- no improvement at all
a ValueError -- swapping two adjacent panels breaks the permutation
slides.why: Identical permutation, identical adjacent-swap neighborhood, so identical result: 0.0925, exactly Monday's verified number.
slides.teaching: Take a quick show of hands before revealing — some will guess the recap 'must' behave differently on a new day; nothing about the date changes a deterministic function's output.

slides.title: [3] Recap: neighbors(), written out in full
slides.explainBody: Monday showed this function; here it is in full, with a loop that prints what it actually produces. neighbors() is a GENERATOR FUNCTION — yield, not return — handing back one adjacent-swap arrangement at a time. Six bays means five adjacent pairs, so five neighbors. Four of the five are WORSE than the starting cost of 0.2325; only [0, 1, 2, 4, 3, 5] at 0.1925 improves, so that is the single move hill climbing will take first. Note the missing return type hint: a generator does not return a list — it yields one list at a time — so it is the one function in this studio without one, on purpose.
slides.teaching: Have students find the one improving neighbor in the printout before the next cell runs — hill_climb takes exactly that move, then repeats the same scan.

slides.title: [3] Recap: define the hill climber
slides.explainBody: min(..., key=cost) checks all five adjacent-swap neighbors. If even the cheapest neighbor is no better, the function returns the current local optimum.
slides.teaching: Ask what best_c >= cur_c means before running the function: no allowed neighbor improves the current solution.

slides.title: Run the recap: the same local trap
slides.code:
end, end_cost = hill_climb([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
print('stuck:', end, 'cost:', round(end_cost, 4))
slides.explainBody: The deterministic function reproduces Monday's local result. Today's genetic algorithm searches beyond that adjacent-swap trap and repeatedly reaches the known 0.0125 solution.
slides.teaching: Keep this result brief, then transition to population search. Call 0.0125 best known unless a proof is supplied.

slides.title: GA building blocks, recapped

left.head: Selection + crossover
left.body: Sort the population by cost; keep the best few as SURVIVORS. Combine two survivors with order crossover — keep one parent's segment, fill the rest from the other parent's order — so every child stays a valid permutation.

right.head: Mutation + the loop
right.body: With some probability (mutation_rate), swap two random positions in a new child. Repeat — sort, select, crossover, mutate — for a fixed number of generations; that whole cycle is one generation.

slides.teaching: This is a recap, not new material — move quickly, and let the next three cells do the actual teaching by running code.

slides.title: [4] Build order_crossover
slides.code:
import random
def order_crossover(parent1: list, parent2: list,
                    rng: random.Random) -> list:
    """Keep a segment of parent1, fill from parent2."""
    size = len(parent1)
    a, b = sorted(rng.sample(range(size), 2))
    child = [None] * size
    child[a:b + 1] = parent1[a:b + 1]
    fill = [g for g in parent2 if g not in child]
    idx = 0
    for i in range(size):
        if child[i] is None:
            child[i] = fill[idx]
            idx += 1
    return child
slides.explainHead: Segment first, then fill the gaps in order
slides.explainBody: Two cut points are drawn and sorted, so a comes before b. The child starts as six None slots; parent1's segment between the cuts is copied in unchanged. fill = [g for g in parent2 if g not in child] is a LIST COMPREHENSION — 'for each gene g in parent2, keep it only if it is not already somewhere in child.' The final loop drops those into the remaining None slots, left to right. That construction is what guarantees a valid permutation, unlike the AI-drafted crossover coming later this studio.
slides.teaching: Trace the fill list by hand on the board: parent2 minus {1, 2} = [5, 4, 3, 0], dropped into the empty slots left to right.

slides.title: [4] continued: run one crossover and check it
slides.code:
p1 = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
p2 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]
rng = random.Random(7)
child = order_crossover(p1, p2, rng)
print('child:', child)
print('valid?', sorted(child) == list(range(6)))
slides.explainHead: A segment kept, the rest filled in order
slides.explainBody: random.Random(7)'s 7 is a random SEED — a fixed starting number that makes this draw reproducible, so everyone in the room sees the same child. It picked cut points (1, 2), so the child keeps parent1's values there (1, 2). fill is parent2 with 1 and 2 removed — [5, 4, 3, 0] — dropped into the empty slots left to right. The last line is the check that matters: every panel index appears exactly once.
slides.teaching: Trace the fill list by hand on the board: parent2 minus {1, 2} = [5, 4, 3, 0]. Then require the True on the last line before anyone moves on.

slides.title: Anatomy: the line every hand-trace depends on
slides.code: child[a:b + 1] = parent1[a:b + 1]

parts.label: The child being built
parts.body: Starts as [None] * 6 above; this line fills part of it.

parts.label: Cut points a, b
parts.body: Chosen just above by rng.sample(...) — the SAME a, b on both sides.

parts.label: Segment source
parts.body: This parent gives one unbroken segment, copied as-is.

parts.label: Source side
parts.body: The repeated a:b + 1 pulls the matching segment from parent1.

slides.teaching: Point at each chip in order, then have students find this exact line inside cell [4] before Studio 3's hand-trace.

slides.title: [5] Build swap_mutation
slides.code:
def swap_mutation(perm: list,
                  rng: random.Random) -> list:
    """Swap two random positions in perm."""
    perm = perm[:]
    i, j = rng.sample(range(len(perm)), 2)
    perm[i], perm[j] = perm[j], perm[i]
    return perm

child = [5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 0]
rng2 = random.Random(3)
mutated = swap_mutation(child, rng2)
print(mutated, sorted(mutated) == list(range(6)))
slides.explainHead: One swap, still a valid permutation
slides.explainBody: rng2 picked positions (1, 4); swapping them turns [5,1,2,4,3,0] into [5,3,2,4,1,0] — still six distinct panel indices, just two of them exchanged, which the printed True confirms. perm = perm[:] copies first, so the caller's list is never modified. rng.sample always returns two DISTINCT positions, so the swap is never a silent no-op, and a swap can never create a duplicate or a gap.
slides.teaching: Have students confirm sorted(mutated) == [0,1,2,3,4,5] out loud before moving on — the property that matters most, stated explicitly.

slides.title: Studio 3: trace crossover and mutation by hand
slides.prompt: Before trusting cells [4]-[5], prove you can trace them on paper.
steps: By hand, apply order_crossover with cut points (1, 2) to parent1=[0,1,2,3,4,5], parent2=[5,4,3,2,1,0].
Confirm your hand-traced child matches [5, 1, 2, 4, 3, 0].
By hand, swap positions 1 and 4 in that child.
Confirm your result matches [5, 3, 2, 4, 1, 0].
slides.teaching: This is the one hand-tracing exercise worth insisting on — everything after this cell is 'run and interpret,' not 'trace by hand.'

slides.title: Predict: does building it yourself change the answer?
slides.code:
best = genetic_algorithm(seed=1)
print('best permutation:', best, 'cost:', round(cost(best), 4))
slides.question: You built both functions. Does seed=1 still reach 0.0125?
options: No -- a hand-built version will drift a little from Monday's demo.
Yes -- generation 9 reaches 0.0125 exactly, and it never leaves that value.
Yes, but only approximately -- something close to 0.02, not exactly 0.0125.
No -- it gets stuck at 0.0925, same as hill climbing.
Yes, but a different permutation than brute force's.
slides.why: Same functions, same seed, same parameters, so the identical verified result: 0.0125 by generation 9, matching brute force exactly.
slides.teaching: This is the payoff moment — the result is not a coincidence, it is the same deterministic math as Monday's demo, now built by the students' own hands.

slides.title: [6] The full GA loop, assembled
slides.code:
def genetic_algorithm(seed: int, pop_size: int = 12,
                      survivors: int = 5,
                      mutation_rate: float = 0.35,
                      generations: int = 30) -> list:
    """Evolve permutations; return the best one."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    population = [list(range(6))
                  for _ in range(pop_size)]
    for ind in population:
        rng.shuffle(ind)
    for gen in range(generations + 1):
        population.sort(key=cost)      # SELECTION
        if gen in (0, 5, 9):
            print('gen', gen, '-> best cost',
                  round(cost(population[0]), 4))
slides.explainHead: Setup, then the first half of one generation
slides.explainBody: Four defaults sit in the signature — population 12, 5 survivors, mutation rate 0.35, 30 generations — so genetic_algorithm(seed=1) reproduces this studio's exact run. population starts as pop_size copies of [0,1,2,3,4,5], each shuffled by the seeded rng, so every individual is a valid permutation from the start. Inside each generation, population.sort(key=cost) puts the cheapest arrangement first — that sort IS the selection step, and cell [8]'s AI draft breaks exactly this line by slicing a list it never sorted.
slides.teaching: Point at population.sort(key=cost): key=cost tells sort to score each individual with your own cost() and order by that score. Everything on the next slide depends on this list already being in order.

slides.title: [6] continued: elitism, crossover, mutation
slides.code:
elite = population[:survivors]
        next_gen = elite[:]        # elitism
        while len(next_gen) < pop_size:
            p1, p2 = rng.sample(elite, 2)
            # CROSSOVER: your function from cell [4]
            child = order_crossover(p1, p2, rng)
            # MUTATION: your function from cell [5]
            if rng.random() < mutation_rate:
                child = swap_mutation(child, rng)
            next_gen.append(child)
        population = next_gen
    return population[0]
slides.explainBody: Because the population was just sorted, population[:survivors] really is the best 5 — and copying them into next_gen unchanged is ELITISM (defined two slides from now). The while loop refills the population back to 12 by drawing two elite parents and calling YOUR order_crossover from cell [4], then YOUR swap_mutation from cell [5] on about 35% of children. rng.random() returns a float in [0, 1), so '< 0.35' is true roughly 35% of the time. Nothing here is abbreviated: 12 - 5 = 7 new children are built every generation.
slides.teaching: Point at 'elite = population[:survivors]' — this exact line is what the upcoming elitism definition slide explains. Count the while-loop's 7 iterations out loud.

slides.title: [6] continued — run it with seed=1
slides.code:
best = genetic_algorithm(seed=1)
print('best permutation:', best,
      'cost:', round(cost(best), 4))
slides.output:
gen 0 -> best cost 0.1025
gen 5 -> best cost 0.0225
gen 9 -> best cost 0.0125
best permutation: [0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1] cost: 0.0125
slides.explainBody: By generation 9 the GA's best individual already matches brute force's (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1), cost 0.0125 exactly — and it never leaves that value through generation 30, because SELECTION always keeps the best 5 individuals.
slides.teaching: Pause on 'gen 9' — remind students this is the SAME 0.0125 from cells [1]-[2], reached a completely different way.

slides.title: Early convergence trace, seed=1 (generations 0–12)
slides.chartTitle: GA best cost through generation 12; generations 13–30 are omitted and flat
slides.yTitle: Best cost x 1000 (axis scaled for readability)
slides.explainHead: The early trace contains the whole change
slides.explainBody: Cell [6] printed checkpoints 0, 5, and 9; the chart fills in generations 0–12. Values are scaled x1000 for readable labels. The best cost reaches the brute-force optimum at generation 9. Generations 13–30 are omitted because elitism keeps the same optimum, so the remaining trace is flat.
slides.teaching: Name the displayed range and omitted flat tail explicitly, then ask why elitism prevents the best-so-far cost from rising.

slides.title: Elitism, defined
slides.definition: Copying the best-scoring individuals from one generation directly into the next generation, completely unchanged, before any new children are created by crossover or mutation.

example.head: elite = population[:survivors]
example.body: In cell [6], the sorted population's best 5 become next_gen's first 5 entries verbatim (next_gen = elite[:]) — so the population's best cost can only hold steady or improve, generation to generation. That is exactly why the chart above never rises.

slides.note: Elitism only guarantees the best-so-far never gets WORSE. It does not guarantee reaching the TRUE optimum quickly, or at all — Monday's seven-seed table showed this same elitist GA reaching 0.0125 anywhere from generation 4 to generation 20.
slides.teaching: Point back at the chart's never-rising shape — elitism is the one-word mechanical reason for it, not a coincidence.

slides.title: Studio 4: confirm the GA reached brute force's answer
slides.prompt: A GA result is only trustworthy once checked against a known answer.
steps: Confirm the best permutation printed above matches brute force's (0, 2, 4, 5, 3, 1) exactly.
Compute individuals evaluated to reach generation 9: 12 + 9 x 7.
Compare that number (75) to brute force's 720 - what percentage is it?
State one sentence: does 75 vs. 720 mean the GA is always 'better'? Why or why not.
slides.teaching: Expected: 75 / 720 is about 10%. Expected answer to step 4: no — Monday's cross-seed table showed this is verified for THESE parameters/seeds, not guaranteed in general.

slides.title: GA vs. brute force: evaluations AND wall-clock time
rows: instrumented count required (do not infer from new candidates)
slides.callout: Compare actual objective-function calls with an instrumented counter. Population size × generations or 'new candidates' can miscount repeated, cached, or reevaluated candidates.
slides.teaching: Be honest that the timing numbers are machine-specific and will vary slightly run to run — the evaluation-count comparison is the portable, trustworthy one.

slides.title: When is the extra machinery worth it?

left.head: Not yet, at N=6
left.body: At N=6, brute force is shorter and easier to audit, and it provides an exhaustive baseline for the encoded problem. It can still be wrong if the candidate generator or cost function is wrong.

right.head: Yes, once N grows or evaluation gets expensive
right.body: 12 panels (12! is about 479 million permutations) or a cost function that takes seconds to evaluate (a real simulation, not a formula) both make brute force impossible — exactly when a GA's far-fewer-evaluations property starts to matter.

slides.teaching: This is the required 'discuss when the extra machinery is worth it' component of this week's assignment — have students write their own one-paragraph answer now, referencing their own Project 2 problem if one applies.

slides.title: Predict: is this crossover safe for a permutation?
slides.question: Given two valid permutations, is the child always valid?
options: Yes -- slicing at a fixed cut point always keeps all 6 panel indices.
No -- whichever panels happen to fall on each side of the cut, duplicates and gaps are likely.
Yes, but only when parent1 equals parent2.
No -- this line raises an IndexError for any 6-element input.
Yes, but the child is always parent1 reversed.
slides.why: Copied from a generic list-GA tutorial that never had to keep a permutation valid: on 200 random pairs it made an invalid child 188 times.
slides.teaching: Have students predict BEFORE seeing the full AI-audit reveal over the next two slides — most will assume 'slicing lists' is always safe, since it was safe in every Week 1-11 script that did not require a permutation.

slides.title: [7] AI-audit, part 1: the crossover and mutation bugs
slides.code:
def ai_crossover(parent1, parent2):
    cut = 3
    return parent1[:cut] + parent2[cut:]

def ai_mutate(perm, mutation_rate, rng):
    perm = perm[:]
    if mutation_rate:                 # any nonzero rate is 'truthy'
        i, j = rng.sample(range(len(perm)), 2)
        perm[i], perm[j] = perm[j], perm[i]
    return perm
slides.explainHead: Two bugs already, before the loop even starts
slides.explainBody: (1) ai_crossover is a single-point crossover copied from a generic list-GA tutorial — on a permutation it produces an invalid child about 94% of the time (verified separately, 188 of 200 test pairs); a fixed cut=3 keeps whichever panels happen to land on each side, so duplicates and gaps are likely. (2) `if mutation_rate:` tests the TRUTHINESS of 0.35 (always True) instead of drawing a random probability, so mutation fires on every child, not at a 35% rate.
slides.teaching: Have students name bug 1 and bug 2 here, before the next slide reveals the third (selection) and the final broken output.

slides.title: [7] AI-audit, part 2: the selection bug and the result
slides.code:
def ai_genetic_algorithm(seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    population = [list(range(6)) for _ in range(12)]
    for ind in population:
        rng.shuffle(ind)
    for gen in range(10):
        survivors = population[:5]   # never sorted!
        next_gen = survivors[:]
        while len(next_gen) < 12:
            p1, p2 = rng.sample(survivors, 2)
            child = ai_mutate(ai_crossover(p1, p2),
                              0.35, rng)
            next_gen.append(child)
        population = next_gen
slides.explainHead: The third bug: selection that never selects
slides.explainBody: (3) `survivors = population[:5]` slices without ever sorting by cost first, so 'survivors' are 5 arbitrary individuals — selection never actually happens. Compare it directly to cell [6], where population.sort(key=cost) runs before the identical slice. The rest of the loop is shown in full here, nothing elided: the while-loop calls the two broken functions from the previous slide, so every child is built by a crossover that does not preserve permutations and a mutation that fires every single time.
slides.teaching: Require students to name all three defects (two from the previous slide, one here) before the next slide runs it — each one individually looks plausible, which is exactly the point of the exercise.

slides.title: [7] continued: run the broken GA, then check validity
slides.code:
best = min(population, key=cost)  # no check
    return best, round(cost(best), 4)

result = ai_genetic_algorithm(seed=1)
print(result)
print('valid permutation?',
      sorted(result[0]) == list(range(6)))
slides.explainHead: Runs with no error — and returns an impossible facade
slides.explainBody: All three bugs compound. min(population, key=cost) reports whatever scores lowest with no check that it is even a legal arrangement, so [0, 3, 4, 5, 4, 1] comes back labelled 'best' at cost 0.0525 — but sorted([0,3,4,5,4,1]) is not [0,1,2,3,4,5]: panel 4 is assigned to TWO bays, and panel 2 is never installed anywhere. Only the last line, comparing against a known-valid structure, exposes it.
slides.teaching: Ask which of the two printed lines a hurried reader would trust — the cost number looks like progress (0.0525 beats the identity arrangement's 0.2325). The False is the only line that tells the truth.

slides.title: Studio 5: diagnose and repair the AI-generated GA
slides.prompt: This function ran with no error — and returned an unbuildable facade.
steps: Name the crossover defect: why does slicing at a fixed cut point break a permutation?
Name the mutation defect: what does `if mutation_rate:` actually test, and why is it always true here?
Name the selection defect: what does `population[:5]` return if population was never sorted?
Rewrite the function using order_crossover, a proper `rng.random() < mutation_rate` check, and a sort-then-slice - confirm it now reproduces 0.0125.
slides.teaching: Require the repaired version to actually run and print 0.0125 before accepting the fix — 'identified the bug' and 'fixed the bug' are graded separately this week.

slides.title: Predict: faster or slower than generation 9?

rng = random.Random(3)
# same GA loop as cell [6], seed changed to 3
slides.question: Seed=1 reached 0.0125 at generation 9. Where does seed=3?
options: Earlier -- by generation 4
The same -- generation 9, like seed=1
Later -- generation 13 or after
Never -- it gets stuck at a different, worse cost
Earlier, but at a different, better cost than 0.0125

slides.title: [8] Self-check: does the GA transfer to one new seed?
slides.code:
rng3 = random.Random(3)
population3 = [list(range(6)) for _ in range(12)]
for ind in population3:
    rng3.shuffle(ind)

history3 = []
for gen in range(31):
    population3.sort(key=cost)
    history3.append(round(cost(population3[0]), 4))
    if history3[-1] == 0.0125:
        break
    elite3 = population3[:5]
    next_gen3 = elite3[:]
slides.explainHead: Same algorithm, new seed, one extra record kept
slides.explainBody: This is cell [6]'s loop written out inline with seed=3 instead of 1, plus one addition: history3 records the best cost at every generation, not just at three checkpoints. The early break stops the loop the moment the recorded best equals the known true optimum, so len(history3) - 1 is the generation it was first reached. Comparing a ROUNDED cost to 0.0125 matters — the raw float is 0.012499999999999994 and would never test equal.
slides.teaching: Point out explicitly that faster-or-slower convergence is expected to vary by seed. This one additional run probes seed sensitivity; it does not guarantee behavior for every seed.

slides.title: [8] continued: rebuild each generation, then report
slides.code:
while len(next_gen3) < 12:
        p1, p2 = rng3.sample(elite3, 2)
        child = order_crossover(p1, p2, rng3)
        if rng3.random() < 0.35:
            child = swap_mutation(child, rng3)
        next_gen3.append(child)
    population3 = next_gen3

print('seed=3 history:', history3)
print('reached true optimum at generation:',
      len(history3) - 1)

slides.explainBody: The rebuild step is your own order_crossover and swap_mutation from cells [4]-[5], called with rng3 so the whole run is reproducible. seed=1 (cell [6]) reached 0.0125 at generation 9; seed=3 reaches the SAME true optimum at generation 4 — faster this time, still the identical answer. This is exactly the kind of different-scenario check this week's assignment requires, not a repeat of the seed=1 demo.
